content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's core identification — faith as trusting faithfulness, i.e., reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience — is directly carried by the verses printed with the entry. Habakkuk 2:4's underlying emunah genuinely denotes faithfulness/steadiness (the book's first-use argument from Exodus 17:12, steady hands, is philologically sound and widely acknowledged even in mainstream lexicons). Hebrews 11:8 states that by faith Abraham 'obeyed,' fusing the trust and the obedience in one clause; Hebrews 11:1's 'substance/evidence' language fits a faith that is produced and examined in conduct. James 2:17 and 2:22 explicitly say faith without works is dead and that 'by works was faith made perfect' — statements the book reads at face value while the trust-only counter must soften into fruit-language external to faith itself. Crucially, the book pre-empts the strongest objection (Romans 4:4-5; Ephesians 2:8-9) by distinguishing works-as-wage-claim (excluded) from works-as-enactment (constitutive of living faith's maturation), and Ephesians 2:10, printed with the entry, supplies exactly the sequence the book claims: saved through faith, created unto good works. The strongest counter — classical fiducia, trust that receives and only subsequently bears works as fruit — does not deny the same referent; it disputes whether fidelity belongs to faith's identity or only to its consequence, and it affirms with the book that works do not purchase the promise and that faith without works is dead. Since both cores can be true of the same referent and the book explains Hab 2:4, Heb 11:8, and Jas 2:22 with fewer interpretive steps, the book wins the comparison. The accepted prior finding on belief (received testimony that submits) independently supports the parallel structure. Every clause of the printed entry is carried by the printed texts, so support is FULL.","book_core_identification":"Faith is trusting faithfulness: reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience — trust and fidelity as one disposition, in which works do not purchase the promise but enact faith and bring it to maturity, such that faith without works is dead.","book_secondary_elaborations":["The emunah first-use argument from Exodus 17:12 (Moses' steady hands) as the paradigm picture of faithfulness","The four-offices scheme distinguishing faith from love, knowing, and belief within one covenant response","The definition of 'works' as commandment-shaped deeds via Exodus 18:20, Psalm 111:7, and Revelation 2:26","The reading of Hebrews 11:1's 'evidence' as something produced and examined in the life","The claim that hope's object is specifically the resurrection, eternal life, the city, and Christ's appearing"],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The classical Reformation fiducia reading: faith is receptive trust in God and in Christ's saving work — notitia, assensus, fiducia — which is the sole instrument of justification and is conceptually complete without works; obedience is the necessary fruit and evidence of living faith but is not part of faith's identity. On this reading Romans 4:4-5's contrast between 'him that worketh' and 'him that worketh not, but believeth' shows that faith is defined precisely by its distinction from doing, and James 2 speaks only of faith's demonstration, not its constitution.","counter_core_identification":"Faith is trusting reliance on God/Christ that receives justification apart from any works; obedience and faithfulness are consequences flowing from faith, external to what faith itself is.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_NARROWER","material_core_denial":"The counter does not deny that faith is trusting reliance on God's promise, nor that living faith issues in obedience, nor that faith without works is dead; it denies only that faithfulness-through-obedience belongs to faith's identity rather than to its fruit. Both identifications can be true of the same referent — a trust that, when living, is held steady in obedience — so there is no material contradiction of the book's core, only a dispute over the boundary between faith and its expression.","counter_case":["Romans 4:4-5 pointedly contrasts working and believing: 'to him that worketh not, but believeth... his faith is counted for righteousness' — suggesting faith's essence excludes doing","Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is through faith 'not of works,' guarding faith's receptive character","Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as assurance and conviction — inner states — before any act is named","The Pauline justification texts (Rom 3:28; Gal 2:16) function best if faith is a receiving instrument distinct from all human performance","James 2 can be read as concerning the demonstration of faith before men ('shew me thy faith'), not the definition of faith before God"],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Habakkuk 2:4's emunah lexically means faithfulness/steadiness, not bare trust; the book reads the very verse Paul builds on (Rom 1:17) in its native sense, while the counter must translate emunah as something narrower than it means","Hebrews 11:8 makes obedience the content of the faith-act ('by faith Abraham... obeyed'), and the whole of Hebrews 11 is a catalog of visible acts — the book explains why the faith chapter is an obedience chapter","James 2:22's 'by works was faith made perfect' says works mature faith itself, not merely display it; the book takes this without strain, the counter must gloss 'perfect' as 'shown'","The book absorbs the counter's best texts rather than colliding with them: Romans 4:4-5 excludes works as wage-claim, Ephesians 2:10 supplies works as the created purpose of the saved — the book's distinction between purchasing and enacting is drawn from the printed verses themselves","The accepted prior premise on belief (receiving God's testimony in a response that submits) establishes the same trust-obedience structure for the cognate verb, making the book's noun-side reading structurally coherent","The first-use pattern (Exodus 17:12, emunah as steady hands) gives an Old Testament anchor consistent with the book's demonstrated method of deriving definitions from the Law and the Prophets"],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Romans 4:5's explicit 'worketh not, but believeth' antithesis reads most naturally if faith and doing are categorically distinct in the forensic context of justification","The counter preserves a cleaner conceptual line for why justification is by faith alone, avoiding any appearance that human fidelity contributes to acceptance with God","It matches the dominant historical exegesis of Ephesians 2:8-9 and the confessional notitia-assensus-fiducia framework"],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Habakkuk 2:4 (emunah = faithfulness, the verse Paul quotes for the faith doctrine)","Hebrews 11:8 ('by faith Abraham... obeyed' — obedience as the faith-act itself)","James 2:17, 22 (faith without works dead; by works faith made perfect)","Romans 4:4-5 with Ephesians 2:8-10 (works excluded as purchase, supplied as created purpose — the book's distinction drawn from the printed texts)","Exodus 17:12 (first occurrence of emunah as steadiness held over time)"],"unresolved_objections":["Whether Romans 4:5's 'worketh not, but believeth' antithesis shows that in strictly forensic justification contexts pistis carries a purely receptive sense that the book's fused 'trusting faithfulness' definition flattens","The pistis Christou debate (faith in Christ vs. faithfulness of Christ) is not engaged by the supplied evidence and could reshape how the Pauline texts bear on the definition","The four-offices scheme's sharp division of labor between faith, love, knowing, and belief is a systematizing elaboration not itself demonstrable from the printed verses"],"confidence":"medium"}
